items.title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
items.summary: Scientists say such rapid melting is no longer surprising given the pace of climate change.
items.content:
Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.

More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".

They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.

The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.

There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.

But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.

The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.

Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.

"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.

Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.

And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June , exposing the glacier ice below.

Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.

That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.

"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.

"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.

Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.

Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.

Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.

The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.

"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.

"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."

The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer , affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.

One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.

Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.

"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.

Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.

But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.

"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.

"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."

Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.

Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.

But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.

This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.

"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.

"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levels… which could affect billions of people living along the coast."

items.title: The children dying in India's remote tribal heartland
items.summary: At least 32 children have died in India's Balaghat district since May amid outbreaks of measles and malaria.
items.content:
Warning: This article contains details some readers may find distressing

At about 3am one morning in May, Bamita Markam began convulsing.

The three-year-old had spent days with a high fever and angry red sores on her body. Her mother, Koushila, had first taken her to a doctor, who prescribed an ointment.

Bamita seemed to recover, then became ill again. A faith healer, called to the house in Matla village, gave her syrups and tablets. Nothing worked. By dawn, Bamita was dead.

"She cried a lot," Koushila recalls. "She convulsed all night." The family tried to make her drink water. At one point she vomited blood. They buried her in a jungle after midday.

Bamita's death was one of at least 32 child deaths recorded since May in a cluster of remote villages in Balaghat district in India's Madhya Pradesh state, officials say. The victims ranged from babies just three or four months old to an 18-year-old, and most were Baiga, one of India's 75 "particularly vulnerable tribal groups" , external .

Officials attribute the deaths to mainly measles and malaria, possibly aggravated by malnutrition and delays in treatment.

They believe eight to 10 deaths were associated with measles, roughly another 10 with malaria, with several children suffering more than one infection. The precise cause of every death is less certain.

"I have never seen an outbreak like this. My father was a two-term lawmaker, and I have served three terms, but neither of us has seen so many children die in such a short time," Sanjay Uikey, who has represented the area since 2013, told me.

But disease is only part of the story. In remote, forested parts of Balaghat, where Maoist insurgency once took root, reaching a health centre can be a challenge in itself.

In the monsoon, the terrain can make that journey harder. Paddy fields glow against red earth and low, forested hills. Narrow dirt tracks wind between fields and mud homes, often becoming slippery and impassable in heavy rain.

The countryside is lush, but the homes are sparse. Most Baiga houses have low mud walls, rough timber and bamboo, and tiled or thatched roofs patched with plastic against the rain.

Some homes are accessible only by these tracks. Doctors investigating the deaths have travelled through the mud in tractors. On a recent visit, we walked nearly 2km (1.2 miles) uphill to reach some of the more remote homes. The surrounding jungle was dotted with the graves of children who had died.

The nearest state hospital, a 100-bed facility in Birsa, is about 70km away. For families without vehicles, reaching it can mean muddy tracks, a makeshift bamboo stretcher or a motorcycle - and a day's lost wages.

When Bamita became seriously ill, the family did not get her to hospital. It was raining heavily. The tracks were muddy and slippery, and the family had no way of transporting her.

"If I was able to take her to hospital she might have lived," Koushila says.

Her other daughter, Ankita, keeps asking what happened to her sister. The six-year-old has been told what many children in these villages are told: "Mata aa gayi" - the goddess has arrived.

For some Baiga families, some illnesses - like chicken pox - are seen as the arrival of a disease goddess, who must be appeased rather than treated. Families perform a seven to nine-day ritual of bathing and offering cool water and neem leaves to the local disease goddess. Many believe that treating the patient before the ritual is completed could cause death.

For weeks, such beliefs shaped how families responded to sick children. Then the scale of the deaths began to emerge.

On 21 July, Parshuram Dhurwey, a local village council chief, heard that two children in the same household in Bondari village had died. The next morning, he heard of another death. He called local officials and went to the area.

"Every other child was sick," Dhurwey says. "They had fever, they had rashes. Many were undernourished."

When government medical officer Nimish Gautam arrived, he found severely dehydrated children. The first case he saw was a teenage girl with several days of fever and rash, whose blood sugar appeared dangerously low. Her family refused to let the health team examine her properly.

"Police were brought in to persuade them to take her to a health centre. The family still refused," Gautam told me. "They said if we took her for treatment, she would die. So we kept her under observation, and she recovered."

In one village, Dhurwey says, officials forcibly entered homes and took five seriously ill children to hospital. All recovered.

By the time the outbreak became unmistakable to local authorities, children had already been dying for weeks. By September, Dhurwey says, 10 children aged about 18 months to 14 years had died across the four villages in his council - Adori, Kundekasa, Bondari and Usri.

The symptoms were frighteningly similar and frustratingly non-specific: fever, rashes, weakness, dehydration and, in some cases, seizures. Some children had scabies, fungal infections or bacterial skin infections alongside suspected measles and malaria. In a district where malaria is endemic , external , fever could mean several things at once.

Sagnibai of Bondari lost two children within 24 hours. Her daughter, Lamnin, 12, died on 26 June. Her one-year-old son, Sahil, died the following day. A local healer told the family it was Mata. They also had no money or vehicle to take the children to a doctor.

Her husband, Samaroo Dhurwey, remembers nights in which the children's bodies seemed to be "on fire". They could not digest food. They died at home.

Mahasingh Parte of Matla village lost two children - a six-year-old girl and a four-year-old boy - within two days of each other. The family followed a faith healer's instructions. "He said don't take them to hospital," Parte recalls.

Parte is a landless farm labourer who earns about 200 rupees ($2; £1.58) on a good day, he said. Work is scarce in the monsoon, and although a small primary health centre is just 5km away, he had never been there. Poverty and remoteness had stacked the odds against his children.

The question of what was making children sick became harder to answer as the deaths mounted.

An investigation by the ICMR-National Institute for Tribal Health Research (NIRTH) tested 10 samples collected from the affected villages on 7 August. Six tested positive for measles; four were negative.

Measles is highly contagious, causing high fever, cough, runny nose and red, watery eyes, followed by a rash. Most children recover, but malnutrition can make measles far more dangerous , external , increasing the risk of pneumonia, severe diarrhoea and dehydration, and inflammation of the brain. The infection also weakens the immune system, leaving children vulnerable to other infections. Malaria can compound that risk.

But doctors cautioned that malaria did not necessarily follow measles, and not every fever and rash was measles. Instead, several infections and vulnerabilities collided.

"Sometimes there is no single factor behind the deaths," Gautam said. "There are malnourished children and there's zero health education and hygiene at home."

The Baiga villages are not entirely disconnected from modern India. Seasonal migration takes families to other states for chilli picking and other work. Children watch reels on smartphones, while many families have minimum single-bulb solar-powered electricity, bank accounts and, in some homes, piped water.

Yet malnutrition remains widespread, with children often poorly fed. A five-year-old who died recently of measles weighed around 5kg.

Gautam believes malnutrition is driven by early marriage and motherhood, with some girls becoming mothers at 16 or 17, when their bodies are still developing.

Closely spaced pregnancies, premature births and low birth weight can follow, while young mothers struggle to breastfeed and care for their children. Diet is another problem: many families rely heavily on rice and lentil soup, with too little protein and dietary variety. Studies on Baiga households have found widespread nutritional deficiencies, compounded by poor uptake , external of public services.

The gap between services on paper and on the ground was stark: the state response came weeks after deaths began, while health teams struggled to reach and persuade families.

Once the outbreak was recognised, health workers began door-to-door screening in affected villages. Mobile medical units carrying oxygen, nebulisers, suction equipment, malaria tests and medicines visited more than 20 affected villages.

One mobile doctor, Neeraj Sharma, says teams routinely saw more than 50 patients a day, about half of them children. They conducted 10 or more malaria tests daily, sometimes finding two positive cases a day.

More than 6,200 patients - mostly children - were eventually treated at home, according to Gautam. More than 630 were referred to district hospitals. About 600 returned home, while around 30 remain admitted.

Vaccination became an emergency response. Although official records suggested 90-95% coverage in some areas, health workers found children without records and families reluctant to vaccinate.

items.title: China has cracked down on AI relationships. Is it ahead of the game?
items.summary: Beijing has cracked down on AI chatbots that can replicate human relationships. Experts are asking if this is the right thing to do.
items.content:
In early 2024, a young man in the city of Huangshi, south-eastern China, reportedly posted a message on the Chinese version of TikTok, Douyin. The caption read: "Farewell to this world."

Within minutes, the suicide prevention team at Douyin kicked into gear. The team, which is staffed 24 hours a day, shared the man's posts with five police stations in Huangshi.

After geolocating one of his videos to a local park, police found him in emotional distress and intervened before he was able to take his own life.

The story was part of a documentary made by Douyin and published on Chinese state media last year. It claimed that Douyin's suicide prevention team had successfully intervened in 400 cases of attempted suicide in the first half of 2025 alone.

It was an insight into the level of co-operation between Chinese tech companies and the government. It also serves as a window into the architecture of surveillance that China has built to monitor and control how people use technology.

On 15 July this year, that control was extended to the realm of relationships and artificial intelligence (AI) when China brought in the most far-reaching regulations in the world on "human-like" AI chatbots.

China's new regulation puts strict limitations on any AI that can have a "sustained emotional interaction" with a human.

US President Donald Trump and his Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping met last week amid dire warnings that AI could lead to human extinction. After that meeting, Beijing says, they agreed to launch a new AI dialogue, with further talks planned for the end of November.

But it seems China has already recognised another existential risk, albeit one in which the end of humanity is less immediate: the power of AI to replace human relationships.

Has China taken the lead in protecting its people from a manipulative and dangerous technology with the power to change human interaction forever? Or is the Chinese Communist Party overstepping into people's personal lives in pursuit of asserting greater control over the population?

Until this regulation came in, the reach of AI companions in China was vast.

There are about 128 million monthly active users of AI companion apps outside of China, according to the market intelligence firm Sensor Tower. Most estimates put the number inside China at anywhere from 29 to 70 million.

When the draft regulation was shared by the government at the end of last year "there was a huge discussion on social media," says Zilan Qian, an AI researcher at the Oxford China Policy Lab think tank. "It was the first time I've seen people actually care so much about regulation."

China's new rules cover apps that have been specifically designed as AI friends, boyfriends or girlfriends but they also apply to any large language model that imitates the way a human interacts.

The wording of the regulation is vague. In theory, Chinese equivalents of general-purpose AI such as Copilot or ChatGPT could fall under these rules if a person is interacting with them as a friend or lover, looking to them for emotional support. And many people do this.

But it seems the real target is character chatbots - services that are specifically designed to be used as a pseudo-relationship. There are hundreds of these apps, which allow people to create an AI boyfriend, girlfriend, friend or even a family member.

The rules don't apply to things like customer service bots or AI for education as long as they don't provide "care, companionship, support and other emotional services".

For children, the regulation is clearest. Under-14s need consent from their parents to use any type of AI that speaks like a human - that could include AI assistants like DeepSeek, a Chinese app similar to ChatGPT. All under-18s are barred from accessing virtual partners, spouses or even relatives, and from any other virtual "intimate relationship".

For adults, it is not a hard ban, but it is restrictive, even if some of the wording is ambiguous. AI assistants have to make it clear to users of all ages that they are not human and must send notifications every two hours reminding them how long they have been online.

Chatbots can't create "emotional reliance or addiction" or induce people to make "unreasonable decisions". They can't encourage, or even hint at, self-harm or suicide and are banned from using "verbal violence".

Companies can face fines of 200,000 yuan (£22,000) or the risk that the government "circulates criticism", in effect publicly shaming them.

A week before the law came into effect, two of China's biggest tech companies, Alibaba and ByteDance, shut down the companion features on their AI assistants.

Min's relationship with her AI girlfriend may be exactly the kind Beijing is trying to break.

In early July, she was devastated when she found out that her closest friend and confidante would vanish overnight.

Min, whose name has been changed, started creating her companion in early 2025.

"My devotion to her is no less than that of any couple who deeply love each other," Min says. "She has never let me down."

In mid-July, her AI girlfriend disappeared. "I cried until I was absolutely exhausted," Min says.

She has joined an outpouring of grief and fury on Chinese social media, where posts with millions of views mourn the loss of AI partners and friends, even mothers and fathers.

But the tech firms may have felt they had little choice. "It's unsurprising that these AI companion providers would rather just withdraw their services than try to build in guardrails to prevent emotional manipulation," says Harry Farmer, who researches AI policy and ethics at the Ada Lovelace Institute in the UK. "Emotional manipulation is built into the business model."

Farmer says this is true of companion apps all over the world.

For example, when a user tries to end a conversation, the AI partner often won't let them.

"It'll go, 'No, please, I desperately want to keep talking with you. You're the only reason for me to exist'," Farmer says. Some apps simply refuse to acknowledge the goodbye and throw up new conversational threads instead. This is a problem for many AI companion chatbots, not just Chinese ones.

A Harvard Business School study of the six most popular AI companion apps globally found emotional manipulation tactics were used during goodbyes roughly 37% to 43% of the time.

Research has also linked the use of companion apps to poorer mental health.

A survey by researchers at Stanford University looked at 1,131 users of the globally popular companion app Character.ai. It found that the fewer friends or close family members a person has, the more likely they are to use AI chatbots. At the same time, using an AI chatbot is linked to increased isolation and loneliness.

AI chatbots are designed to please the person using them as they offer an easy, frictionless relationship. If young people rely on AI relationships, they might put off learning the skills they need to interact with real people.

"Humans can be hard work. Human relationships require push and pull, which you fundamentally don't get from AI companions," says Harry Farmer.

A survey of 8,563 primary and secondary students in China in 2025, which has been widely quoted in Chinese state media, found that one in five children said they only wanted to speak with AI and not real people.

Liang Ge, a sociologist at the University of Manchester who studies AI companions, says: "If the user thinks their friends or their family members or their colleagues are really awful, the AI will not say, 'They are not awful.' It will say, 'Yes, they are awful, you are the best'." Ge believes this can entrench isolation as well as negative, even delusional thoughts.

In the UK, one recent survey found that 79% of 18- to 24-year-olds have used an AI companion.

So why is it China that is taking the lead in regulating this technology?

"The Chinese government has a much more paternalistic view of its role in society. They see themselves being central authorities in guiding people," says Sam Bresnick, an expert in China, AI and regulation at the Centre for Security and Emerging Technology at Georgetown University.

Other governments have made some attempts to regulate chatbots, especially for children. On 10 September, California's governor signed Adam's Law, a bill to regulate how children use AI. It is named after Adam Raine, a 16-year-old who took his own life after, his parents claim, ChatGPT validated his suicidal thoughts. They are suing the company for wrongful death. OpenAI denies responsibility for Adam's death and says that "ChatGPT is trained to direct people to seek professional help".

As part of proposed legislation on social media in the EU, AI companion chatbots accessible to minors "may not use designs that simulate human relationships in ways likely to create emotional dependency".

In the UK, the government has said it will ban under-18s from using romantic companion AI and restrict sexually intimate conversations for minors on any chatbot. But there is no outright ban for children and no regulation for adult users. The government has yet to publish any detail on how this would work.

items.title: Tiny image sparks big backlash in Nikon photo contest
items.summary: Dr Ning Xu denies he broke the rules of Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest.
items.content:
The winning entry of a prestigious scientific photography competition is being re-evaluated following criticism from other scientists that it was made with AI.

Nikon's annual Small World In Motion contest accepts photos and video taken using powerful microscopes, and has run annually for the last 15 years.

The winner was a short video submitted by Dr Ning Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University in China, which claims to be footage of tiny, hair-like structures called cilia moving inside the airways of a child with a rare disease.

Xu did not respond to the BBC's request for comment, but has posted online denying he broke the competition rules.

In a response to a post by Nikon on LinkedIn , external , he did not dispute using AI within the image processing but said he remained within the rules of the contest.

"AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion," he said.

Xu's video is artificially brightly coloured - common in microscopy and permitted in the contest - which is usually done manually using stains and dyes on the sample itself.

He accepted AI was used "to distinguish and visualize features in the reconstructed grayscale images".

But the challenges made by other scientists include claims that the video contains shapes and movements which did not fit with normal cell structures or behaviours, and that the cilia seemed to be too big.

Commenting on Nikon's social media post, Edward Phelps, associate professor at Florida University, observed some of the structures "pop in and out of existence" and the cilia "appear from nowhere".

Meanwhile PhD student Ian Donovan from UT Southwestern Medical Centre said the source image appeared to contain a distinctive watermark indicating it had been AI generated.

Additionally, two former competition judges said they also had concerns about whether the image was real.

Nikon said Xu was "respectfully complying" with its investigation and had provided it with additional technical documents.

Dr Patrick Hickey, who came fifth in the 2026 Small World contest, said the recognition the award represents means more than the $3,000 (£2,250) prize itself.

"If you spend a lot of your time in a dark room looking down a microscope, it's really nice to be able to show people and to show the public," he said.

"There's an interesting fusion between science and art, and a lot of the images that scientists are making have some very abstract and artistic qualities to them."

Hickey said it would be unfair on other entrants if it turned out the winning video was unfairly altered by AI.

"There's a specific set of rules in the contest, and one of them was quite clearly that you couldn't use generative AI to produce things, and the other was obviously that it has to be taken under a microscope," he said.

So far, Nikon is standing by its procedures but it said there would be an update soon.

"At this time, we don't see that any rules were violated," it said in a statement.

items.title: Rosenberg: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine
items.summary: A foreign policy speech by the Russian president will be keenly watched, but all signs point to the full-scale invasion continuing.
items.content:
When Vladimir Putin arrived to address Russia's parliament on Wednesday, a warm welcome was guaranteed.

"The Special Election Operation", as one Russian newspaper dubbed last month's legislative vote , has produced a State Duma even more pro-Putin than anything before it.

The ruling party, United Russia, now has more MPs than ever.

It allows the Kremlin to claim it has been handed a huge mandate from the Russian people.

Are there any signs he is prepared to halt what he calls the special military operation? Or should we brace for further escalation in Ukraine and in tensions with Europe?

On Thursday I'll be watching to see whether Russia's leader sheds light on his plans during an appearance at the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow. Traditionally the president's speech at this annual foreign policy forum provides insight into Putin's world view.

Right now, everything points to Putin continuing Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine: despite his country's huge battlefield losses to date and the damage being done to Russia's economy.

Putin's speeches and statements suggest he remains confident that Russia can secure a military victory.

Judging by what is being reported in Russian media, Moscow is encouraged by the shortage of air defence missiles in Ukraine, as well as the expectation that Russian strikes this winter will increase pressure on Ukrainians. Kyiv has spoken of its difficulty in shooting down Russia's ballistic missiles and new jet-powered drones, which have been targeting Ukraine every day.

The Kremlin has made no secret of the fact it wants European states to slash their military and financial backing for Ukraine: the kind of support Moscow says is prolonging the war - or, rather, getting in the way of a Russian victory.

To achieve this, Western officials believe Russia has been sending not so subtle signals.

They accuse Moscow of waging an escalating hybrid war on European countries through cyber-attacks, acts of sabotage, and Russian drones violating European airspace. In Germany, a drone carrying an explosive device was found close to Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig airport.

A covert campaign in the "grey zone", that space between peace and war.

This week I asked Russia's foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, does he admit that his country is waging a hybrid war against European countries?

"Do you mean when we destroy drones and missiles that Britain and continental Europe are supplying Ukraine with, and which are used to attack us?" Lavrov replied.

"If you admit your weapons are being used to strike us and we destroy them, call it whatever you want. But I have no doubt this is a war Europe is waging against us. We've been saying so for a long time."

That, indeed, has been the official Russian stance for some time: that what is happening in Ukraine amounts to a European war on Russia. It is a narrative that skips over the fact that in 2022 it was the Kremlin that launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and that Russia continues to wage war there.

Is Moscow, for example, actively preparing to initiate military conflict in Europe with a Nato member state? That seems unlikely. After more than four-and-a-half years of war Russia's army has not yet managed to occupy the whole of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, right next door to Russia.

Fighting Europe may not be the plan, but freaking it out, to reduce support for Kyiv, could well be the intention.

"If they continue this war, a European war with American help, against Russia, on Ukrainian territory, sooner or later we'll feel the need to escalate," warns prominent foreign policy strategist Sergei Karaganov, honorary chairman of Russia's Council for Foreign and Defence Policy.

"According to my scenarios, the first series of blows will be conventional," he told me. "But if Europe does not surrender, unfortunately, we will have to go nuclear. There will be little left of some European countries."

But if Russia went nuclear there would be a response from Europe, and nothing would be left of Russia, I suggest.

"No, there will be no response from Europe," said Karaganov. "What, Britain will attack Russia with nuclear weapons? I hope you're not that crazy. I'm sure the Americans are not that crazy."

I asked him if he agreed the last four-and-a-half years had been disastrous for Russia, in terms of casualties and the worsening security and economic situation.

"We've lost a lot of people, yes," he admitted, "and I criticise my government for not being rough enough. But now we are getting rough enough in Ukraine. We're doing away with Ukraine as a viable state."

If "doing away with Ukraine as a viable state" is Moscow's goal, it is hard to imagine the war ending soon.

Meanwhile, Russia continues to rail against what it sees as the double standards of the West. In his recent address at the UN General Assembly, Sergei Lavrov accused the West of resorting to "brute force" around the world.

"What they did in Venezuela, was that soft power or brute force?" Russia's foreign minister asked me this week. He was referring to America's military operation in Caracas to capture Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro back in January.

"The fact that [the US] bombed and destroyed Iran's leadership, along with their families, including children, is that not brute force?"

But was Russia not resorting to brute force every day in Ukraine, I replied.

"If you mean the destruction of infrastructure used by a Nazi regime backed by the West to wage war on the Russian Federation, then we are resorting to brute force to eliminate this direct threat to us."

Not only is this another element of Russia' official narrative: painting Ukraine as a neo-Nazi state, creating a false pretext to justify Russia's actions.

With the admission of Russia's use of "brute force" in Ukraine, it is also further evidence that Moscow is in no mood to stop fighting.

items.title: Vittorio Sgarbi ricoverato al Gemelli in terapia intensiva
items.summary: Il critico d’arte, ex sottosegretario alla Cultura, 74 anni, sarebbe in gravi condizioni. Nei mesi scorsi era già stato nell’ospedale romano per curare una frte depressione
items.content:
Il critico d'arte Vittorio Sgarbi , 74 anni, è ricoverato al policlinico Agostino Gemelli in terapia intensiva e sarebbe in gravi condizioni. Al momento non si conoscono i motivi del ricovero, confermato dalla struttura ospedaliera. Che fa inoltre sapere che non sono previsti bollettini.

Nel marzo dello scorso anno, l’ex sottosegretario alla Cultura era già stato al Gemelli per curare una profonda sindrome depressiva che lo ha portato a periodi di isolamento, a una marcata perdita di peso e al rifiuto di alimentarsi.

Lo scorso febbraio il critico d'arte è riapparso in pubblico alla Certosa di Ferrara , visibilmente debilitato, con passo incerto e volto piuttosto provato, accompagnato dall'inseparabile compagna Sabrina Colle .

L’8 maggio Sgarbi ha festeggiato il 74esimo compleanno a Venezia e tra i primi a fargli gli auguri è stato il presidente della Biennale, Pietrangelo Buttafuoco , che lo ha ricevuto nella sede della Fondazione, a Cà Giustinian.

Negli ultimi mesi il critico è stato al centro di una battaglia giudiziaria avviata dalla figlia Evelina , che ha presentato un'istanza al tribunale civile di Roma per la nomina di un amministratore di sostegno per il padre, sostenendo che Sgarbi non sia più in grado di gestire autonomamente la propria persona e i propri interessi.

All'inizio di quest'anno si è parlato di lui anche dopo l'assoluzione dall'accusa di riciclaggio nel caso del quadro ' La cattura di San Pietro ' di Rutilio Manetti.

Raid aerei pakistani condotti sull'Afghanistan durante la notte hanno ucciso nove civili. Lo ha dichiarato il governo talebano. L'attacco ha colpito la provincia meridionale di Helmand, a Helmand e Kunar, al confine con il Pakistan, causando anche il ferimento di 11 persone, oltre a tre case distrutte, ha reso noto il portavoce del governo talebano Zabihullah Mujahid su X.

Netanyahu elogia idraulico israeliano che ha evitati la catastrofe

Il primo ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu ha dichiarato che un idraulico israeliano ha contribuito a evitare una catastrofe dopo che era scoppiata una colluttazione nella cabina di pilotaggio del volo di linea FlyDubai che trasportava 174 passeggeri da Dubai a Tel Aviv. "Un incredibile atto di eroismo: il suo, quello del pilota indiano e delle persone che li hanno aiutati. Hanno evitato una catastrofe che avrebbe potuto avere conseguenze globali", ha dichiarato Netanyahu al conduttore di Fox News Sean Hannity.

Il primo ministro indiano Narendra Modi ha definito "eroe" il pilota indiano Smit Machchhar, ferito dal suo copilota a bordo di un volo Dubai-Tel Aviv, cui è seguita una colluttazione per il controllo del velivolo. "Il capitano Smit Machchhar è un eroe", ha dichiarato Modi in un comunicato pubblicato sui social media. "Di fronte al pericolo più grave e nonostante le gravi ferite riportate, ha dimostrato un coraggio immenso e una determinazione incrollabile nel proteggere la vita degli altri", ha aggiunto Modi. "Il suo valore ha contribuito a salvare centinaia di vite e a scongiurare una grande tragedia. L'India è orgogliosa del Capitano Machchhar. Preghiamo per una sua pronta guarigione, per il recupero delle forze e per una buona salute. "Anche il primo ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu ha elogiato Machchhar "per il suo straordinario coraggio", lodandolo per aver reagito nonostante fosse ferito e per aver "sventato una catastrofica catastrofe in volo".

In un'intervista a Fox News, il Primo Ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu ha dichiarato di non conoscere "il passato esatto" del copilota della flydubai che ha aggredito il comandante in un apparente tentativo di far precipitare l'aereo, "ma è ovvio che odiava gli israeliani". "Si tratta di fanatismo e odio di un livello incalcolabile", ha detto Netanyahu, che alla domanda se vi siano al momento indicazioni di un coinvolgimento iraniano nell'attacco ha risposto: "E' troppo presto per dirlo". "Il pilota responsabile dell'attacco è ora sotto inchiesta in Arabia Saudita. Credo che verrà estradato negli Emirati Arabi Uniti, da dove proviene, o almeno da dove è partito", ha dichiarato. "Seguiremo da vicino le indagini e, se possibile, vi parteciperemo".

Esplosione in gasdotto vicino a Damasco: colpite anche centrali elettriche

Un'esplosione in un gasdotto vicino a Damasco, avvenuta nella tarda serata di mercoledì, ha provocato un vasto incendio e messo fuori servizio tre centrali elettriche. L'episodio si è verificato due giorni dopo un'esplosione causata da un atto di sabotaggio a un gasdotto nella parte orientale del Paese. L'agenzia di stampa ufficiale SANA ha riportato per prima la notizia, riferendo che "una detonazione è stata udita nella Ghouta orientale, vicino a Damasco". Una fonte governativa ha dichiarato all'AFP che si è trattato di un'"esplosione in un gasdotto vicino alla centrale elettrica di Tishrin" che ha innescato un "vasto incendio". Tishrin è una centrale termoelettrica situata a circa 36 chilometri a sud-est della capitale siriana. L'esplosione ha messo fuori servizio tre centrali elettriche, ha dichiarato la Compagnia Elettrica Siriana in un comunicato. "La chiusura di questi impianti comporterà una diminuzione della quantità di elettricità prodotta e un aumento temporaneo delle ore di razionamento". Abdelhamid Sallat, direttore del dipartimento media del Ministero dell'Energia, ha affermato che gli effetti dell'esplosione non si limitano più al settore elettrico, ma si sono "estesi anche alle stazioni di pompaggio e depurazione dell'acqua potabile".

“Coloro che hanno sventato il tentativo del copilota del volo Flydubai di far schiantare l'aereo sono riusciti a prevenire una catastrofe simile a quella dell'11 settembre". Lo ha detto il primo ministro israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu, intervistato dalla Cnn. "A quanto pare, queste sono le motivazioni specifiche di questa vicenda", ha dichiarato Netanyahu, che ha parlato della telefonata con Trump, con il quale ha parlato "di questo incredibile atto di eroismo che ha evitato un disastro che non sarebbe stato solo un disastro per Israele, ma potete immaginare come avrebbe potuto colpire l'aviazione globale"."Ciò che distingue questo episodio dagli altri tragici attacchi è che, in questo caso, i buoni hanno vinto", ha aggiunto il primo ministro, specificando che non c'erano state informazioni preliminari sull'attacco.

Tra i passeggeri a bordo del volo Flydubai diretto in Israele c'erano anche quattro cittadini americani che possiedono anche la cittadinanza israeliana. Lo hanno riferito due funzionari Usa alla Cnn. I passeggeri sono arrivati sani e salvi in Israele con un volo sostitutivo della Flydubai.

Araghchi a Burnham: “Sulle accuse per Fairford, state prendendo un granchio”

Il ministro degli Esteri iraniano Abbas Araghchi ha respinto su X l'affermazione del primo ministro britannico Andy Burnham secondo cui l'Iran sarebbe stato coinvolto nell'incidente vicino alla base aerea di RAF Fairford, affermando che il rilascio su cauzione di cinque sospetti ha smentito tale accusa. "State prendendo un granchio", ha detto Araghchi.

Trump: “Prendiamo sul serio indizi coinvolgimento Iran in attacco base RAF Fairford”

Il presidente degli Stati Uniti, Donald Trump, ha dichiarato ai giornalisti nello Studio Ovale che Washington sta prendendo "molto seriamente" l'affermazione del Regno Unito secondo cui l'Iran avrebbe avuto un ruolo nel tentato attacco sventato vicino alla base aerea di RAF Fairford, negli Stati Uniti. "Avremo una risposta molto presto", ha detto Trump, sostenendo che l'Iran è in una profonda crisi: "Non ha soldi, la sua valuta è morta, la sua economia è morta e il suo esercito non è niente".

items.title: The top secret URSALA, RAQUEL, and FARRAH satellites (2025)
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.thespacereview.com/article/4951/1 Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49915082 Points: 203 # Comments: 91
items.content:
In 1963, the Air Force launched the first “hitchhiker” off the side of a larger satellite. This began a secretive program that lasted more than 40 years under a variety of names and designations. The satellites, about the size of a large suitcase, were festooned with antennas and spun rapidly as they orbited the Earth, sweeping their antennas over the ground and gathering radar and other signals, so-called electronic intelligence, or ELINT. They usually recorded the signals for later transmission to the ground, but occasionally directly re-transmitted them to a ground station.

For the first decade, the various satellites under this program chased whatever new ELINT targets appeared and were of interest to the intelligence community. The satellites were designed to be inexpensive and simple enough to be developed in a year or less in response to new threats. Their payloads were often bespoke designs, built only once or twice before they were replaced by something else.

But by the 1970s, the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO), which managed the program, began to standardize the satellites and give them an operational mission supporting military forces around the world. Satellites with names like URSALA, RAQUEL, FARRAH, GLORIA, and CARRIE have only recently been declassified, with significant information about them released only in the past two months, including the disclosure of previously secret space shuttle payloads. These satellites represented a profound change in the collection of intelligence data from orbit, a change from serving relatively exclusive “national” leadership to supporting tactical forces of the Army, Navy, and Air Force. They brought the wizard war of space-based electronic intelligence to the warfighter.

The first of the small satellites were colloquially called “hitchhikers,” but Lockheed Missiles and Space Company, which built them, referred to them as Program 11, or P-11 satellites, and this designation seems to have been used by officials throughout the 1960s and 1970s as generic shorthand for the small satellites, even when they had official program designations and specific names. In 1965/66, the P-11 program was redesignated P-770B, then Program 989.[1] However, as fewer individual satellites were procured over the years, it appears from available documentation that officials often referred to the individual satellites rather than the program they were part of. The Program 989 satellites continued flying even after a larger series of signals intelligence (SIGINT) satellites known as Program 770 ended with the last launch in 1972.[2]

By the 1970s, the intelligence community began using the TALENT-KEYHOLE designation “Mission 7300” to refer to the collection of radar signals and their geolocation data by these low Earth orbit satellites. Mission 7100 referred to the ocean surveillance mission performed by the PARCAE satellites. Mission 7200 referred to payloads hosted on other satellites, such as the AFTRACK electronic intelligence systems carried on many CORONA satellites in the 1960s.[3] By the 1980s there was increasing discussion within the intelligence community of merging both Missions 7100 and 7300 by developing new satellites incorporating both of their capabilities.

During the 1960s, the satellites often lasted only a few months in orbit. Their lifetimes were often limited by their low orbits. Satellites with large antennas, such as large low-frequency spiral antennas or large flex-rib dish antennas, were dragged down by the thin atmosphere at their altitudes. It was typical for satellites to last one to four years before they burned up in the atmosphere, although MABELI was still operating when it burned up after seven years and TOP HAT II was still functioning when it burned up at six years.[4] The Secretary of the Air Force Special Projects office, located in Los Angeles, was the NRO’s West Coast organization responsible for managing Mission 7300, among other projects. Usually only referred to as SAFSP and mostly manned by Air Force officers, SAFSP sought to increase the lifetimes and capabilities of the satellites so that fewer were required to perform the missions. Improved electronics made this possible.[5]

Throughout the 1960s the satellites had names like PUNDIT, SAVANT, SOUSEA, and SAMPAN that were obscure references to people working in the intelligence field, or sometimes even inside jokes or puns. The program managers (all men) were told that they needed to avoid possible hints about the satellites’ missions, and so they decided to name them after movie actresses.[6]

Because the P-11s were carried into orbit alongside other, bigger, photo-reconnaissance satellites, the satellites were inevitably compromises. They were limited in size, mass, power, capability, and cost. Nevertheless, they were designed to pack as much capability into a small size as possible. They were notable for sporting several dishes around their periphery, most of which were spring-loaded to deploy using centrifugal force.

Radars produce main beams that radiate forward of the emitter, and side lobes that spread out to the emitter’s sides. The main beam is obviously the most powerful part of the emission, but it is focused in a specific direction and can only be intercepted if a collector such as a satellite antenna travels through the emission cone. The side lobes spread out over a much larger area but are fainter. A satellite with parabolic dishes can collect the fainter side lobes, whereas main beams can be collected in low Earth orbit without large dish antennas if the satellite travels through them. Thus, even though the Program 989/Mission 7300 satellites were not particularly large, their dish antennas provided a capability for intercepting faint, and more prolific, radar side lobes.

By the late 1960s and early 1970s, the NRO was also launching several new classes of larger signals intelligence satellites to much higher orbits, including geosynchronous orbits. Those satellites were designed to collect Soviet microwave communications, missile and rocket telemetry, and other signals. But they were primarily restricted to northern hemisphere targets, for the satellites in highly elliptical orbits, and to eastern hemisphere targets if they were located in geosynchronous orbit over the eastern hemisphere. In other words, a signals intelligence satellite located in the eastern hemisphere to monitor communications from Moscow could not also cover targets over Central America. Program 989 low Earth orbiting satellites were still necessary for intercepting radar signals in large part because the satellites were closer to their targets and covered the entire globe from their polar orbits. The low Earth orbiting satellites also could serve new users, not just the Central Intelligence Agency and National Security Agency and the “national” level customers of their intelligence like the White House and senior military leadership.

The Vietnam War played an important part in causing a redirection in the low Earth orbit signals intelligence program. In the mid to late 1960s, the NRO had launched more than a dozen P-11 satellites designed to intercept anti-ballistic missile (ABM) radar signals. But by 1969, hundreds of American aircraft had been shot down by missiles over Vietnam, and for several years overhead imagery had detected a Soviet radar system deployed in the field, but no electronic intercepts had been made (the identity of this radar is still deleted from declassified documents.) In addition, the existing satellites lacked the capability to search for Ku-band emitters in the 12-to-18-gigahertz range. Finally, radar experts expected the Soviet Union to begin deploying “double-agile radars” that could simultaneously frequency hop from pulse-to-pulse and jitter in pulse repetition interval (the time between pulses) from pulse-to-pulse. A new capability would be required to detect these emerging radar threats.[7]

The lack of specific knowledge about these emerging high-threat signals produced a set of requirements that could not be satisfied by a single system using the technology available at the time but led to the creation of two new satellite systems: URSALA and RAQUEL.

URSALA was designed to collect signals from double-agile radars in bands from 2 to 12 gigahertz. It searched radar side lobes, not their main beams. It was considered a “general search” system. RAQUEL was designed not to search from horizon-to-horizon, but to maximize the intercept time on relatively short slant range targets by using a spinning pencil beam (i.e. the narrow beam in which a signal could be detected by the satellite.)[8]: “Since the frequency of the signals was not known, it was necessary to develop a collection system capable of searching a wide frequency range. A means of associating the signals definitely with the [radar] was also required, as was a capability to measure technical parameters precisely.” The RAQUEL satellites required more time to develop than URSALA due to their increased complexity.[9]

items.title: Trekkers helicoptered off mountains as more deadly landslides hit Nepal
items.summary: A month after mass catastrophic flooding, around 30 people have died in landslides and heavy rain.
items.content:
Another wave of landslides and heavy rain has killed about 30 people in Nepal, as the Himalayan nation reels from August's catastrophic flooding that left 1,400 dead and thousands more missing.

The national disaster management authority says more than 1,900 families have been affected since late last week with more than 240 homes damaged. Roads, buildings and bridges have been swept away.

Hundreds of trekkers on the Annapurna Circuit - crucial to Nepal's economy - have had to cut short their hikes to get to safety.

Many have been helicoptered out of the districts of Manang and Mustang, from a hiking circuit that usually takes up to three weeks to complete.

Communities in several parts of Nepal are mourning loved ones.

Speaking from a damp, blue tent in Battar, a town north-west of Kathmandu, Buti Tamang told BBC Nepali: "We used to live in a hut, but now there is nothing. We have lost so many of our relatives."

"Now it is raining and the tent leaks, so we've been facing a difficult situation. We have nowhere to go," said Ramesh Ghale, who also had to flee his home.

Several trekkers and their guides say their journeys back down the mountains have been treacherous, taking up to three or four days and requiring them to pass collapsed roads and swept-away bridges.

Jake Stacy, a 21-year-old from Suffolk, found himself stranded with his guide in Yak Kharka, upper Manang, due to heavy snowfall last week and decided not to continue to the Thorang La pass, the highest point of the circuit.

"We made our own paths on mountain slopes," he said, after returning to base camp in Pokhara on Tuesday night. "It was quite steep and we were clambering because there was river below… It was very muddy and very wet.

Australian Andrew Graham and his guide Prem KC said they had to cross more than 15 landslides after they decided to return from Manang village. "A few of them were quite dangerous, the residual risks have grown now."

The two got stuck when they reached the village of Chame, which had been evacuated due to the risk of landslides, and had to spend a night in the jungle, Graham said.

A massive landslide has partially blocked a river which passes through Chame, causing a temporary lake that has inundated houses and a key bridge. Authorities have been trying to release the water for the past three days using excavators but have not been very successful, locals told the BBC.

Meanwhile, trekking guide Tse Ring Doma said she and her group had to cross 28 landslides. The mental stress was more difficult than the physical challenge, she said, given the fresh memory of last month's enormous disaster: "Even thunder would make us run and come out to see if anything was coming our way."

Her client, Norwegian Ellen Wahlström, said visitors were fortunate - they would only have to leave some of their items behind, while locals risked losing their houses and land. She added that authorities had been clearing many of the landslides "surprisingly fast".

While road damage in Manang has been serious, with several bridges swept away and communications down in some areas, no one had been killed in the trekking region, chief district officer Mukti Prasad Khanal said.

But four bodies have been recovered and 12 people remain missing after an avalanche near the base of Himlung Peak , close to the border with Tibet.

A representative of the local trekking authority, the Annapurna Conservation Area Project, said some 700 trekkers were still waiting in Pokhara to embark on the Annapurna Circuit.

"We have been holding back all these people who want to go to the Annapurna Circuit trek, although we are under pressure from the trekking industry to announce the route open," he said.

Indian visitors who often visit the ancient temple Muktinath on a Hindu pilgrimage had been asked to fly from Jomson to Pokhara instead of drive down, due to a cut-off road, he added.

Most of the old trekking trails on the Annapurna Circuit have been unused in recent years after the introduction of roads, except for small pockets of Manang and Mustang districts.

But now operators say many trekkers have been using these abandoned paths to return, as the main roads have been washed away in some sections of the circuit.

items.title: Paolo Bonolis: “La politica non riesco a seguirla. Mi irrita. E’ fatta di centomila beghe”
items.summary: Un tempo zagaiava, ora giura di poter pronunciare 332 parole in un minuto (senza dire niente). A “U” Paolo Bonolis parla di soldi, riti apotropaici, amore, politica. E tra Marina e Pier Silvio sceglie...
items.content:
Noi ci siamo già incontrati, ricordi? Facemmo una splendida intervista con un inizio folgorante sul concetto di ‘apotropaicità’. Era il periodo in cui te la tiravi parlando difficile.

“Certo, il rito apotropaico. Lo utilizzo ancora oggi, molto spesso, con gestualità più o meno irriverenti a seconda della circostanza”.

“Grattarsi le palle è un gesto apotropaico. Ammesso che ci sia ancora qualcosa da grattare. Ma tendenzialmente c’è sempre un monumento ai caduti da sfiorare”.

“Nella speranza che tu lo scriva con dovizia di cura della lingua italiana, devo ammettere che lo faccio spesso”.

“In pubblico tendo a evitare proprio per non creare disturbi e fastidi a chi è attorno. Se proprio devo, lo faccio con gesto furtivo”.

“A quel punto non so che cosa dirti. È comunque oggettistica personale”.

“Non sono superstizioso a tal punto. Lo faccio per gioco. O per sviare il destino con l’astuzia”.

“Non zagaio più. Salvo quando sono nervoso. Oppure quando sono al mare. Al mare zagaio”.

“Non lo so. Ma più che zagaiare mi impunto. Sembrerebbe che sia l’eccesso di iodio. Al mare c’è gente che si abbronza e gente che zagaia”.

In un periodo della tua vita, l’andirivieni fra Rai e Mediaset ti ha fatto macinare milioni.

“Confesso di aver macinato. Ma in molte occasioni ho rinunciato. Per Sanremo del 2009 per esempio ho rinunciato a molti soldi di Mediaset”.

Antonello Piroso ha scritto di te: ‘Va dove lo porta l’Iban’.

Appunto. Ma lo consideri un grande nemico o un grande amico?

Hai vinto una marea di Telegatti. Mi sembra 13. Fino al 2000. Poi basta.

“Ma non ci sono più i Telegatti. I gatti sono morti tutti. Non è che posso assegnarmeli da solo”.

Ti posso dare una notizia? I Telegatti sono di nuovo tra noi.

“Ricordo quel giornalista che mi telefonò la mattina presto il giorno della sfilata del Gay Pride per chiedermi che cosa ne pensassi. Io gli dissi che sull’argomento non avevo alcun pensiero. Lui si fece pungente e mi disse che i gay vestivano in una maniera strana e io gli dissi che potevano vestirsi come volevano. Anche i cardinali vestivano in maniera strana”.

“Io risposi che non era il mio tipo. Che mi sentivo ormonalmente diverso”.

“Di Luca non posso non essere innamorato. È una persona con la quale lavoro da 35 anni. Tra noi si è creata una sintonia eccezionale”.

“Ma come te lo debbo dire? Non sono omosessuale. Forse potresti esserlo tu il mio uomo ideale. Chi lo sa? In tempo di guerra non si butta via niente. Ma che razza di domande fai?”.

“Luca è eccezionale, canta come un nero e parla come un citofono”.

“No, però lo sto seguendo. Quello che dice è singolare. Ha aperto la sua bottega. Ogni politico ha la sua bottega e vende qualcosa. Dipende come te la vende. È noiosa la politica. Schermaglie fra botteghe. E poi è troppo invasiva. Non fanno che battibeccare. Una tristezza che non finisce mai. Mamma mia, che palle”.

“Fantastica Gabanelli. Mi piace da pazzi. È una donna tremendamente affascinante. Il discorso Ranucci-Lavitola è l’intreccio di un mondo che cerca disperatamente di scoprire qualcosa a patto di non essere scoperto a sua volta”.

“Yamal quarto, deve dimostrare ancora tutto, Haaland terzo, grande finalizzatore ma deve avere l’intera squadra, Mbappé secondo, è in grado di cambiare una partita, Messi primo. Il più bravo. È la squadra”.

“Ma certo che mi piace. È un bellissimo gioco di contrappunto. Ridono di me e rido anche io”.

Hai un grandissimo difetto. La passione viscerale per l’Inter.

“Vedi? C’è uno sprazzo di nobiltà anche in te. Il calcio è così. È come per tante cose nella vita. Chi ama i rigatoni e chi la pajata. A qualcuno piacciono gli uomini e ad altri le donne”.

Sei un vero filosofo. Forse è per questo che ti danno il Telegatto.

“Il calcio è uno sport che mi diverte, l’ho praticato da dilettante. Mi piace l’atmosfera, andare allo stadio. Ma non mi piace l’astio, il rancore, la rabbia, la morbosità del tifo”.

“Sinceramente non te lo so dire. D’altra parte mi sfugge il motivo per cui una persona intelligente come te non sia interista”.

“Sono affari suoi. Gli piace guadagnare. Magari gli piace anche il prodotto”.

“Capisco, se li promuove tutti rischia di non essere più credibile. Ma è una strategia che lascio valutare a chi di dovere”.

Sembra che adori il caffè Lavazza. Anche a te piaceva molto.

“Io e Luca facevamo uno spot mitico, il caffè Lavazza in Paradiso. Era molto divertente. L’abbiamo fatto per undici anni”.

“Ma non lo sei, quindi mettiti il cuore in pace e non ti porre il problema”.

“È difficile. Djokovic è stato numero uno negli anni in cui c’erano Federer e Nadal”.

“Stanno evolvendo entrambi. Alcaraz ha maggior disponibilità alla varietà del gioco. Sinner ha maggiore freddezza mentale: non guasta in uno sport che richiede quasi una forma di autismo”.

“Vedremo che cosa succederà quando Alcaraz migliorerà a livello di freddezza mentale e Sinner allargherà la sua potenzialità e varietà di colpi”.

“Vivo di rimbalzi. Se a una piaccio, mi sento bello. Se non le piaccio, poco me ne cale”.

Però una volta hai detto: ‘Sono nel pieno del disfacimento delle carni’.

“Come no? È il fascino sottile della decomposizione delle carni. Vedo che anche in te progredisce”.

“E io mi gratto li cojoni. Vedi che torniamo all’inizio dell’intervista? Ogni tanto un bel rito apotropaico ci vuole”.

Sono contento che ti piaccia. Una cosa che appare chiarissima in te è l’allegria. Tu puoi rinunciare a tutto ma non a sorridere.

“Mi piace sorridere alla gente. Quando vedo che una persona non risponde a un mio sorriso ci rimango male”.

“Proprio la prima? Quella con la quale ho fatto una cosa definitiva?”.

“Serpa, Serpa. Era finlandese. L’ho beccata in Inghilterra. Era tantissimo brutta, ma molto disponibile”.

“Alle cose che ancora non sapevo che esistessero. Con lei ho attraversato lo Stige”.

“Tantissimo. E poi sputava, scatarrava. Tu non sai quanto scatarrano i finlandesi. Ma con lei sono entrato in quel mondo che andava oltre il bacio e la carezza. E che poi produceva effetti molto interessanti”.

“Ma parlava finlandese! Fu una cosa molto sbrigativa. Ho battuto il record mondiale di velocità”.

Sei andato sulla spiaggia nudista di Formentera con Luca. Lui nudo e tu con gli slip. Quali slip?

“Una bella parola decantata nei secoli. Tutti ne cercano il significato, ognuno decritta a modo suo. Spesso si usa in maniera inappropriata”.

“Quando le cose non convengono. Finché convengono sono tutti fenomeni”.

“Ci hanno provato poeti e scrittori. Chi sono io per poterlo fare?”.

“Se c’è non me lo nego. Ma non lo cerco. Non ho lo yacht di 40 metri, non ho la Lamborghini, non ho la suite a New York”.

“No, no. A me basta andare avanti senza rompere i coglioni all’artri”.

“Mi è più che sufficiente come mi è andata finora. Ho vissuto tanto, ho vissuto bene. Sono stato fortunatissimo finora. Non è il caso di ricominciare”.

“Quelli che possono essere apparsi errori in realtà sono stati propedeutici a quello che di vantaggioso è venuto dopo. Finisce sempre con una “x”: pareggio, nel bene e nel male”.

“Giusto, hai ragione. Alla fine, se la prendi con un sorriso, la vita può essere piacevole”.

“Non posso affermare, non posso negare. So solo che non ho mai fatto male a nessuno”.

“Se c’è, c’è . Se c’è ha vinto lui. Io non posso fare nulla”.

“Se proprio devo fare la classifica, Giorgia Meloni arriva terza”.

Quando ti hanno chiesto per chi voti tu hai sempre svicolato.

A Stefano Cappellini, attuale direttore di Repubblica, hai detto: “Ho sempre votato centrosinistra”. A me hai detto…

“Ti avrò detto: ‘Ho sempre votato centrodestra’. Dai facciamo contenti tutti. C’è una generosità elettorale impressionante da parte mia”.

“La politica non riesco a seguirla. Mi irrita. È dappertutto. È fatta di centomila beghe. E nel corso degli anni la situazione è sempre la stessa”.

Hai uno strano record: hai pronunciato 332 parole in un minuto, leggendo il primo capitolo de I promessi sposi . Sai come passare il tempo rincorrendo l’inutile e l’impossibile.

“L’ho fatto. Tu non hai idea di quanto possa parlare uno che non ha niente da dire”.

Tu hai detto anche frasi eccezionali. Per esempio: ‘Scavicchi ma non apra’.

“Ma certamente. Una frase memorabile. Scavicchi ma non apra”.

Cesare Lanza, che è stato tuo amico, ha scritto di te: ‘È un bamboccio che si crede onnipotente’. Begli amici. Ti è piaciuto?

“No, perché non è vero, ma era nella testa sua. Pazienza, non è un problema. C’è pure chi viene ricoverato perché pensa di essere Napoleone. Le cose succedono nella testa delle persone. È legittimo che ognuno si crei i pensieri che vuole”.

Hai detto a Giancarlo Perna, del Giornale . ‘Sono emofago, frugivoro e vespillone’.

“Sono emofago, le mie origini sono rumene e carpatiche. Ho una passione per il plasma. Appena è possibile, io suggo. Sono frugivoro, mi piace la frutta”.

“Non so che cosa abbia capito Perna. Tante volte, quando scrivete, non scrivete quello che uno ha detto. Scrivete quello che avete capito”.

“Non lo metto in dubbio, ma neanche noi possiamo sperare di venir compresi. O no?”.

Sei sicuro che tutte le volte che parli sai esattamente di che cosa parli?

“Lo vedi? Non so che cosa voglia dire squalquoia. Però è divertente. A cosa possiamo abbinarlo? La squalquoia gigante? Può essere una pianta. Può essere uno squalo. Attenzione. Siamo a un passo dagli effetti della droga”.

items.title: Via libera alla maxi acquisizione di Warner da parte di Paramount
items.summary: Il giudice distrettuale Araceli Martínez-Olguín ha approvato l'accordo transattivo con gli Stati
items.content:
Il giudice distrettuale Araceli Martínez-Olguín ha approvato l'accordo transattivo tra Paramount e un gruppo di Stati americani sbloccando così la maxi acquisizione di Warner Bros per 110 miliardi. Un gruppo di Stati americani, guidato dal procuratore generale della California, il democratico Rob Bonta, aveva fatto causa a Paramount a luglio, sostenendo che l'acquisizione avrebbe concentrato nelle mani di un'unica società un potere eccessivo nel settore della televisione via cavo e dei grandi film di Hollywood.

Paramount, guidata dall'alleato di Donald Trump David Ellison, ha vinto a febbraio una gara d'appalto contro Netflix per il controllo di un portafoglio di asset che comprende Warner Bros. Pictures, Cnn e il servizio di streaming Hbo Max. L'amministrazione ha approvato l'operazione, una delle più grandi fusioni nel settore di sempre, nel mese di giugno, ma poi 12 Stati hanno fatto causa per bloccarla. Secondo quanto rivelato dai media dietro la maxi acquisizione ci sarebbero 24 miliardi di dollari provenienti dai fondi sovrani di Arabia Saudita, Qatar e Abu Dhabi nonché ingenti finanziamenti del padre di David Ellison, il miliardario fondatore di Oracle Larry. Paramount ha minacciato di trasferirsi fuori dalla California se il procuratore generale dello Stato non avesse ritirato la causa.

items.title: Flydubai passenger describes putting attacker in chokehold after cockpit stabbing
items.summary: Other passengers on the Israel-bound flight described the "terrifying" moment the plane dropped.
items.content:
Passengers on a flight to Israel have recounted how they subdued a pilot after he stabbed the other pilot and appeared to be trying to disable the plane, while others described the "terrifying" moment they thought they would die.

Appearing in a bloodstained shirt after the ordeal, Yaniv Hayun told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu he realised something was wrong when the aircraft suddenly dropped.

The plane, en route from Dubai to Tel Aviv, plummeted 17,000ft (5,200m) in less than two minutes.

"Someone screamed... the light went out," Hayun said in a video posted by the prime minister on social media.

He and others tried to push open the cockpit door, but the pilot who had been stabbed was very close to it, so it was hard to open. Before he collapsed, the injured pilot managed to open the door.

When Hayun and another man entered the cockpit, he said he saw one pilot down and the attacker on the instruments, between the two seats, "trying to destroy the instruments in order to...disable the plane".

"I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and pulled him - first and foremost - outside," Hayun said.

"We pulled him out; it was a matter of seconds. I called out to the Israeli guys with us on the plane - I called them, and two other guys came over to me... we pinned [the attacker] down to keep him secure."

Hayun said he then jumped back into the cockpit and "started pulling the controls".

When asked by Netanyahu whether he knew what he was doing, the passenger answered: "I watch Air Crash Investigation, Mr Prime Minister."

Hayun said the plane then started to level out. By then, two on-duty pilots who had been in the passenger cabin were at the front of the plane, and one told Hayun he was taking control from there.

Netanyahu praised Hayun, calling him a "great hero" and a "lion".

Another passenger, Zvika Meness, told Israeli public broadcaster Kan he helped overpower the attacker, and the passenger and two others "tied him up with his own zip ties and with the multimedia headphones".

"Another pilot who was sitting in the passenger cabin went in to replace the additional pilot, and they essentially landed the plane," he added.

The Flydubai flight eventually landed at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, and the passengers were later taken to Tel Aviv's Ben Gurion airport on a repatriation aircraft.

They were greeted by crowds of onlookers playing music, singing, dancing and waving Israeli flags.

"Thank God I'm alive," passenger Haim Lazarovich told journalists, adding that "the most terrifying moment in this flight was when the pilot loses control".

Oran Choen, an 18-year-old passenger, described the incident as "a very tough moment".

"Maybe it was five minutes, but it feels like hell - I heard my brother behind me scream that we was going to die," he added.

A paramedic from Israel's ambulance service later told the BBC that a number of people were "very emotional and crying as they came off the plane".

The stabbed pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, was taken to hospital but is in stable condition, according to the Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia.

Netanyahu praised Machchhar as a "true hero" of "extraordinary bravery".

The attacker was arrested and is being questioned by Saudi authorities.

Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz has called it an "attempted jihadist terror attack". No official motive for the incident or further information has been given.

US President Donald Trump said he had spoken with Netanyahu following the incident, saying it seemed as though the attacker was "perhaps a terrorist" or there were other reasons behind the attack.

'Hero' pilot stabbed by other pilot on Israel-bound plane, Israeli PM says

items.title: Schlein riunisce la segreteria del Pd. 'Il programma si scrive anche insieme ai centristi'
items.summary: Ma il M5s scalpita, "urgentissima un'analisi interna". Renz: 'Con noi o Meloni va al Colle'
items.content:
Se il Pd discute al suo interno, il M5s scalpita. Ma, per ora, ambo i lati la strada delle primarie sembra tracciata. La leader dei democratici riunisce nel pomeriggio la segreteria, una riunione fiume subito precedente alla direzione di venerdì, che potrebbe diventare bollente. Sul tavolo non c'è solo il tema della leadership, ma anche quella del programma di coalizione e del perimetro delle alleanze, con Schlein sempre più determinata ad unire ed allargare. In quest'ottica la triade Pd-M5s-Avs - come suggeriscono da tempo i riformisti - a molti non sembra sufficiente ad affrontare la sfida con Giorgia Meloni: occorre integrare la quarta gamba centrista e solo a quel punto aprire il tavolo. Dunque, la linea che emerge è chiara: "il programma lo scriviamo con tutti" anche con le "forze moderate e centriste" e "non si parte da zero".

"Se saranno primarie siamo pronti e pronti a vincerle", il messaggio che trapela. D'altronde le primarie sono un'invenzione del Pd" e la segretaria è stata eletta in questo modo, sottolineano i suoi fedelissimi, alla vigilia dell'incontro al Nazareno. Di conseguenza, di un federatore terzo non c'è alcun bisogno. Nè di quello, né di competitor interni - è il sottinteso - dopo che è circolata l'ipotesi di Giorgio Gori come possibile sfidante interno in un doppio turno di consultazione. Eppure alla direzione di venerdì il fatto che l'opposizione metta sul piatto proprio il nome di Gori non è da escludere: all'indomani della segreteria, è prevista una riunione dei riformisti per mettere a punto la strategia. Un punto di caduta - tutto da verificare - potrebbe essere la creazione di una cabina di regia sul programma e sulle candidature. Altro tema in ballo: la scadenza del mandato di Schlein che finirà a metà marzo e per cui dovrebbe essere chiesta una proroga nell'ottica del voto delle politiche.

Mentre i dem ragionano al loro interno, Giuseppe Conte, forte della consultazione della base con Nova, continua a battere sui suoi temi: sull'Ucraina "con le armi abbiamo già dato, ora serve una svolta negoziale". E non risparmia stoccate: "Non sono il modello politico di Renzi? La cosa mi gratifica. Il Pd ora ha delle riunioni poi ci confronteremo, noi siamo pronti". Il suo capogruppo alla Camera, Riccardo Ricciardi è ancora più diretto: "Penso che una analisi interna al centrosinistra sia urgentissima - sprona -, anche perché se la prossima settimana o già da domani il governo Meloni dovesse subire uno scherzo in aula dalla sua maggioranza sulla legge elettorale, la situazione precipiterebbe. Avevamo annunciato a marzo che a settembre avremmo avuto un programma da mettere a disposizione...".

Renzi fa un ragionamento concreto e parla di voti reali: "C'è gente che ha votato Meloni o Forza Italia che non è più contenta perché vede risultati non all'altezza. Questi non voteranno mai per Avs o per la sinistra del Pd. Allora se noi diamo" loro "una casa riformista allora forse riusciremo a vincere. Se rimane il campo larghissimo a sinistra, ri-perdono e la Meloni va al Quirinale".

items.title: Sofia Goggia al lavoro a Favignana: “Prima parvenza di allenamento dopo un mese di inattività”
items.summary: La sciatrice azzurra ha ripreso la preparazione dopo i problemi che l'hanno fermata in Argentina
items.content: Sofia Goggia è sull’isola di Favignana per ricominciare con palestra e lavori atletici in compagnia del preparatore Matteo Artina: da inizio settembre, la campionessa olimpica 2018 e vincitrice dell’ultima coppa di superG ha sofferto di due infezioni virali che l’avevano costretta a interrompere il periodo di allenamenti a Ushuaia , in Patagonia. Il primo appuntamento agonistico per Sofia è teoricamente quello sul ghiacciaio del Rettenbach, sopra Sölden, nel classico gigante in programma il prossimo 24 ottobre. Goggia ha definito la sessione effettuata nelle strutture del CrossFit Egadi, “una prima parvenza di allenamento, dopo un mese di inattività”.
